    Admin Setup

    Mark Padgham

    2026-10-15

    Source: vignettes/admin-setup.Rmd
    admin-setup.Rmd

    This vignette describes the one-time infrastructure steps required to deploy roreviewapi on a Digital Ocean droplet, including the editor volunteer search feature introduced in v0.2. Endpoints for that feature are described in the editor search vignette.

    The Software Peer Review Lead should set up a regular alert system to automatically check the deployment status. This bash script issues an alert if anything is wrong:

    #!/usr/bin/env bash

URL="https://reviewbot.ropensci.org"
status=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" "$URL")

if [[ "$status" != "404" ]]; then
    echo -e "reviewbot is down"
    exit 1
fi

    That should then be regularly called, for example by calling it within a ~/.bashrc file, or via a local cron job.

    Prerequisites

    • SSH access to the Digital Ocean droplet
    • A Postmark account with a verified sender address
    • Access to the AirTable base containing the editor-in-chief rotation table
    • Ability to request DNS records for your institution’s domain

    Environment variables

    Secrets are not stored in the Dockerfile or anywhere else in the git repository. They live in a .env file that exists only on the droplet, is listed in .gitignore and .dockerignore, and is injected into the plumber container at runtime via env_file: .env in docker-compose.yml. Because the file is untracked, git pull never overwrites it, and the values never end up in an image layer.

    Create .env in the project directory on the droplet, with one KEY=value entry per line (no quotes and no export), and restrict its permissions:

    chmod 600 .env
    Variable Description
    GITHUB_PAT GitHub personal access token (also used as GITHUB_TOKEN)
    PKGCHECK_TOKEN pkgcheck authentication token
    GMAIL_SENDER Sender address used for outgoing emails
    GMAIL_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET Path to the Google OAuth client secret JSON file, e.g. /data/email/<client_secret>.json
    GMAIL_TOKEN_CACHE Path to the cached Gmail token, e.g. /data/email/gmailr_token
    GMAIL_AUTH_EMAIL Google account used to authenticate with Gmail
    AIRTABLE_API_KEY AirTable personal access token
    AIRTABLE_BASE_ID ID of the AirTable base containing the EiC rotation table
    ROREVIEWAPI_BASE_URL Public HTTPS base URL of the deployed API (https://reviewbot.ropensci.org)

    At container start, docker-entrypoint.sh writes these values to ~/.Renviron (setting GITHUB_TOKEN from GITHUB_PAT, and ROREV_CONTAINER=true), so that R can read them, and then starts the API. To change a secret, edit .env on the droplet and re-run restart.sh; no change to the Dockerfile is needed.

    The two GMAIL_* file paths must be inside /data/email/, which is the container side of the bind-mounted data directory (see Droplet preparation). Place the corresponding files in /srv/roreviewapi/data/ on the droplet. That mount must remain read-write, because the Gmail token cache is written back during authentication.

    AirTable

    1. Generate a personal access token at https://airtable.com/create/tokens with at least data.records:read scope on the relevant base. Set this as AIRTABLE_API_KEY.
    2. Open the AirTable base and copy the base ID from the URL (https://airtable.com/appXXXXXXXX/...). Set this as AIRTABLE_BASE_ID.

    The editor-in-chief-rotation table within that base must have period_start, period_end, and acting_eic_email fields.

    Droplet preparation

    Create the persistent data directory that will be bind-mounted into the container. This directory holds the SQLite database, the notify-email cache file, and the Gmail OAuth client secret and token cache files, and must survive container rebuilds.

    sudo mkdir -p /srv/roreviewapi/data
sudo chmod 700 /srv/roreviewapi/data

    DNS

    Ask your DNS administrator to add an A record pointing your chosen subdomain to the droplet’s IP address, for example:

    review.example.org.  IN  A  <droplet-ip>

    Allow up to 24 hours for propagation, though it is usually much faster.

    TLS certificate

    Once the DNS record is live, obtain a Let’s Encrypt certificate on the droplet. The --standalone method requires port 80 to be free (stop the running stack first if necessary):

    sudo apt install certbot
sudo certbot certonly --standalone -d reviewbot.ropensci.org

    The certificate and key are written to /etc/letsencrypt/live/review.example.org/. Certbot installs a systemd timer that renews certificates automatically; confirm it is active:

    systemctl status certbot.timer

    Troubleshooting: HTTP-01 challenge failed

    The HTTP-01 challenge works by certbot binding a temporary server to port 80. Two things can prevent this:

    Port 80 occupied. The Docker stack must be stopped before running certbot, otherwise nginx holds port 80 and the challenge fails immediately:

    docker-compose down
sudo certbot certonly --standalone -d review.example.org
docker-compose up -d

    Port 80 blocked by a firewall. There are two independent firewalls to check:

    Droplet firewall (ufw):

    sudo ufw status

    If ufw is active and port 80 is not listed, open it:

    sudo ufw allow 80/tcp
sudo ufw allow 443/tcp

    Digital Ocean cloud firewall: in the DO console under Networking → Firewalls, confirm there is an inbound rule allowing TCP port 80 from all sources. The cloud firewall sits in front of the droplet and blocks traffic before it reaches ufw, so both layers must allow port 80.

    To confirm DNS has propagated before retrying certbot, check that the A record resolves to the droplet IP:

    dig +short review.example.org

    Deployment

    Set NGINX_SERVER_NAME in the environment before starting the stack — this value is substituted into nginx.conf at container startup. Ensure .env exists (see Environment variables), then:

    export NGINX_SERVER_NAME=review.example.org
docker-compose up -d --build

    Routine redeployment is handled by restart.sh, which runs git pull --ff-only, tears down and rebuilds the stack, and brings it back up. It is intended to be called from cron. It locates the project directory from its own path, so it needs no editing, but .env must sit alongside it. Since .env is untracked, secrets persist across pulls.

    The compose file:

    • Mounts /srv/roreviewapi/data into the plumber container at /data/email, and sets ROREVIEWAPI_EMAIL_DB=/data/email/searches.sqlite so the SQLite database persists across rebuilds.
    • Reads secrets from .env via env_file.
    • Mounts /etc/letsencrypt read-only into the nginx container so the certificate is available.
    • Exposes ports 80 (HTTP → HTTPS redirect) and 443 (HTTPS).

    Cron job

    restart.sh is run on a schedule so that the droplet picks up new commits and rebuilds fresh images without manual intervention. One authorized admin of the Digital Ocean droplet needs to configure the cron job.

    The job must run as a user that can run docker-compose (either root or a member of the docker group). The following uses root’s crontab, so that the log file below can be written to /var/log.

    Initial setup

    1. Check whether a job already exists (see “Viewing current jobs” below), to avoid creating a duplicate.

    2. Open the crontab for editing; if prompted, choose an editor (nano is the easiest):

      sudo crontab -e

    3. Add the following line, replacing the path with the absolute path to the project checkout on the droplet:

      0 0 * * 2 /bin/bash /<path>/<to>/roreviewapi/restart.sh >> /var/log/roreviewapi-restart.log 2>&1

      This runs the script at 00:00 every Tuesday. The five leading fields are minute, hour, day of month, month, and day of week (0–7, where both 0 and 7 are Sunday). crontab.guru is useful for checking a schedule. The trailing redirect appends all output, including errors, to a log file.

    4. Save and exit. Cron picks up the change automatically; no restart of the cron service is needed.

    An absolute path is required because cron does not run in the project directory. restart.sh finds the project directory (and thus .env) from its own location, so it needs no other configuration.

    Viewing current jobs

    List the jobs in root’s crontab with:

    sudo crontab -l

    Omit sudo to list the current user’s own crontab instead. Each user has a separate crontab, so if nothing appears, check the other user (or root) that may have been used to set the job up.

    Modifying or removing the job

    Re-open the crontab with sudo crontab -e, edit the line (for example, change the schedule fields), and save. To disable the job without deleting it, comment the line out by prefixing it with #; to remove it, delete the line. Confirm the result with sudo crontab -l.

    Checking that it ran

    Inspect the log file written by the job:

    tail -n 50 /var/log/roreviewapi-restart.log

    and confirm the containers are up with docker ps. To test the job without waiting for the schedule, run the same command by hand:

    sudo /bin/bash /<path>/<to>/roreviewapi/restart.sh

    Transferring maintenance

    Maintenance falls into two parts with very different transfer costs:

    • Operations (deploying, debugging, restarting): needs access only. Nothing in .env changes.
    • Credentials tied to an individual: the Gmail authorization, and the GitHub and AirTable tokens, belong to whoever created them. These must be re-created by the new maintainer if the outgoing person’s accounts will be closed.

    Operations only

    When the new person only deploys and debugs, and the existing authorizing account stays active:

    1. Add their SSH key and sudo access on the droplet.
    2. Add them to the roreviewapi GitHub repository.
    3. Add them to the ro-auto-email Google Cloud project’s IAM.
    4. Hand over this document and the contents of .env (securely, for example via a password manager rather than email or chat).

    Transferring credentials

    This is required if the outgoing maintainer’s accounts will become unusable, for example on leaving the organization. The values in .env that are tied to a person are:

    Variable Tied to Action on transfer
    GITHUB_PAT GitHub account that created it Replace with a token created by the new maintainer
    AIRTABLE_API_KEY AirTable account that created it Replace with a token created by the new maintainer (see AirTable for the required scope)
    GMAIL_AUTH_EMAIL, GMAIL_TOKEN_CACHE Google account that authorized gmailr Replace, following the Gmail transfer steps in the editor search vignette
    GMAIL_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET, GMAIL_SENDER Google Cloud project and the reviewbot@ropensci.org alias Unchanged if the same Cloud project and alias are kept
    AIRTABLE_BASE_ID, ROREVIEWAPI_BASE_URL, PKGCHECK_TOKEN Not tied to a person Unchanged unless the base, URL or pkgcheck service changes

    The steps are then:

    1. The new maintainer creates their own GitHub and AirTable personal access tokens, and completes the Gmail steps in the editor search vignette.

    2. Update .env on the droplet with the new values.

    3. Run restart.sh (or wait for the next scheduled run) so that the container picks up the new .env and credentials:

      sudo /bin/bash /<path>/<to>/roreviewapi/restart.sh

    4. Verify that the editor search workflow still sends and receives emails (see the editor search vignette).

    5. Once the new setup works, the outgoing maintainer should revoke their old GitHub and AirTable tokens, and the old Google grant.

    Other items to update

    • Cron job. If the cron job was set up under the outgoing maintainer’s account, move it to root’s crontab (see Cron job), or recreate it under the new account.
    • Git identity. The git config lines in the Dockerfile hold the user.name and user.email used for commits made inside the container.
    • Uptime alert. Whoever receives the deployment-status alert at the top of this document should be updated.
